title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.
why: This asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver. It connects the computability of arithmetic, logical definability and the existence of rational points on algebraic varieties. The unresolved boundary persists despite undecidability over the integers and decidability of polynomial feasibility over the reals and algebraically closed fields; allowing fractions fundamentally changes the permitted witnesses.

importance.reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.

progress.text: The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem settles the integer-solution problem negatively; rational solvability remains a different decision problem.
Koenigsmann’s Annals paper gives a universal definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\), implying undecidability of the universal-existential fragment but not the purely existential fragment.
Anscombe and coauthors explicitly record Hilbert’s tenth problem over \(\mathbb Q\) as open and review its relation to existential definability.

The height-comparison undecidability paper appears in Journal of Number Theory after its 2023 preprint. It settles an expansion by height predicates, while retaining the ordinary rational question as open.
The Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman article appears online, proving a negative answer over the ring of integers of every number field; its print issue is March 2026.
Poonen’s account reviews the rings-of-integers breakthrough and gives an alternative proof of the relevant Diophantine-definability implication. Its domain restriction remains essential.

status_note: Explicitly open over Q in the cited rational-solvability sources. A bounded primary-source check through 14 September 2026 located no resolution of this exact question. Checked recent results prove undecidability over rings of integers or after adjoining height-comparison predicates; neither settles existence of an unrestricted total rational-solvability decider. This is a formulation and source-scope audit, not an independent verification of every cited proof.

context_blocks.text: Rational tuples can be effectively enumerated and tested by exact substitution, so every YES-instance is eventually recognizable. Such a search does not halt on a NO-instance. The target requires termination in both cases, irrespective of efficiency. A solver for all instances would also allow a rational zero to be found when one exists.

The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem proves that no general algorithm decides integer solvability. It does not automatically decide the rational problem: \(2X-1=0\) has a rational zero but no integer zero. A rational solver cannot simply be applied to the unchanged integer equation.

Allowing rational coefficients gives the same decision problem, because their denominators can be cleared effectively. Finite systems of equations are also equivalent to a single equation: over \(\mathbb Q\), \(f_1=\cdots=f_r=0\) holds exactly when \(\sum_i f_i^2=0\). More generally, disequalities can be encoded using inverse variables and disjunctions using products. These equivalences identify the problem with decidability of the existential first-order theory of \(\mathbb Q\) in the language of rings.

An existential definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\) would transfer integer undecidability to this problem. Koenigsmann’s Theorem 1 instead defines \(\mathbb Z\) by a universal formula; its Corollary 3 establishes undecidability for universal-existential sentences. Quantifier alternation is essential to that conclusion: the full first-order theory and the universal-existential fragment are already undecidable, while neither fact settles the purely existential target.

Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman prove undecidability over the ring of integers \(\mathcal O_K\) of every number field \(K\). Here a number field is a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\mathcal O_K\) consists of elements satisfying a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. This restricts the solution domain; in particular \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Z\), whereas the present question permits every rational number.

Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the recent proof of undecidability for these rings and supplies an alternative definability argument from rank stability. Its Theorem 4.2 concerns definitions over rings of integers. This account does not extend the negative answer to the whole field \(\mathbb Q\).

Garcia-Fritz, Pasten and Vidaux prove undecidability when rational equations are supplemented with finitely many height-comparison conditions. For a rational tuple \(q\), their logarithmic height is \(h(q)=\log\max\{d,|dq_1|,\ldots,|dq_m|\}\), where \(d\geq1\) is its least common denominator, and the added predicates compare heights of tuples. These extra constraints are absent from the target. Their ordinary rational-solvability question remains explicitly open.

sentences: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals asks whether an arbitrary integer-coefficient polynomial has a zero consisting of exact rational numbers.
The target requires one deterministic algorithm that always halts and decides this for every number of variables, degree and coefficient size.
There is no efficiency requirement, and merely enumerating rational solutions does not decide instances with no solution.
Undecidability over integers, universal definitions and results with extra height predicates have different logical or arithmetic scope.
Recent advances over rings of integers preserve that distinction, and the checked sources do not settle the rational-solvability question.
